query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, a uniformly formed, adherent oxide film generated by a controlled pre-oxidation treatment can act as a physical barrier against aggressive humid environments, thereby suppressing the onset of corrosion degradation at room and moderately elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel as received from the manufacturer, exhibiting its native surface condition and microstructural features (including typical grain boundary and dislocation distributions from processing).
generation.intervention: A thermal pre-oxidation treatment conducted in air (for example, heating at 300 °C for 1 hour) designed to promote the formation of a homogeneous and adherent iron oxide layer on the steel surface, compared to an untreated reference.
generation.conditions: Corrosion exposure tests in a controlled atmosphere with high relative humidity (approximately 90% RH) at room temperature (25 °C) and at an elevated temperature (75 °C), with exposures lasting for 168 hours to simulate harsh environmental conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The quality (density, uniformity, adhesion) of the surface oxide film as characterized by techniques such as scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD).
generation.mechanism: The protective oxide film limits transport of corrosive species (e.g., oxygen, moisture, and ions) to the steel substrate. Its formation reduces the number of active sites for localized corrosion (e.g., pitting initiated at grain boundaries or defect sites) by acting as a physical barrier, thereby delaying the initiation and progression of corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The specimens that receive the controlled pre-oxidation treatment will show lower corrosion rates (evidenced by reduced weight loss, less pitting, and higher impedance from electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) relative to the untreated samples under the same environmental conditions.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel in its as-received state (without any additional oxidation treatment).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to tests in high-humidity conditions at room and moderately elevated temperatures. It does not necessarily extend to extreme temperatures or chemically aggressive environments beyond the conditions tested.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent of corrosion suppression (i.e., magnitude of improvement) is uncertain due to possible variability in oxide film formation and the inherent heterogeneities in the steel’s surface; additional variations in processing may influence the reproducibility of the protective effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a comparative corrosion study in which two sets of Q235 steel samples are prepared: one set subjected to the defined pre-oxidation treatment (300 °C for 1 hour in air) and a control set left in the as-received condition. Both sets will then be exposed concurrently in a controlled chamber set to 90% RH at both 25 °C and 75 °C for 168 hours. Periodic assessments (every 24 hours) will be performed.
measurements: Weight loss measurements to quantify overall material loss.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess the integrity of the oxide layer and overall corrosion resistance.
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to evaluate the oxide film’s morphology, uniformity, and phase composition, and to detect pitting or localized corrosion features.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in weight loss, pitting density, or improved EIS response compared to the untreated samples under identical conditions, then the hypothesis—asserting that the controlled oxide film delays corrosion onset—should be rejected.
